title: ECT Is Not What You Think: A Century of Drift from Back Room to Routine Treatment
dek: Modern ECT is a procedure performed under anesthesia and muscle relaxants, with strong efficacy, but the evidence on memory-loss side effects remains incomplete, and social misunderstanding has led to its excessive stigmatization.
why: If your impression of ECT is still stuck on One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest, this episode will completely reset it. Hear the real procedure, indications, side effects, and one expert's clinical account.
who: Clinicians, psychiatric and pediatric staff, medical students, and anyone with doubts about ECT or who wants to understand the evidence behind first-line treatment.
skip: The early history section can be skimmed; but the treatment procedure portion and cases are essential.

points.body: If you or I were to receive ECT, here is how it goes: first a risk assessment and informed consent, then a physical exam, and an overnight fast. The next morning, in the hospital or outpatient clinic, an IV line and two blood pressure cuffs are placed (on the arm and right leg), and EKG, EEG, and EMG are connected. After the anesthesiologist puts you to sleep, the leg cuff is inflated to limit blood flow to the right foot, then a muscle relaxant (such as succinylcholine) is given. Once the muscles are fully relaxed, a bite block is placed, and then a brief electrical current is delivered through electrodes (lasting seconds or even half a second). The goal is not to make you convulse all over, but to induce a generalized seizure, typically lasting 25-70 seconds. Because the muscles are relaxed, you see almost no external movement—the whole process is obvious on the EEG.

points.h: Electrode placement and why the right side
points.body: There are several electrode placements: bitemporal (like in the movies), bifrontal, and most commonly 'right unilateral'—one electrode on the right temple, the other on the right side of the top of the head. Right unilateral is used for most people because it has fewer cognitive side effects. Why consider the right side first? Because for about 98% of right-handed people and 70%-90% of left-handed people, language function is in the left temporal lobe. Avoiding left-sided electrical stimulation theoretically reduces language-related memory problems. But right unilateral is slightly less effective than bilateral. During treatment, doctors switch based on side effects and efficacy: if bilateral side effects are severe, switch to right unilateral; if right unilateral is not effective enough, switch to bilateral.

The seizure threshold is the minimum amount of current that can induce a seizure. There is no precise measuring device; you start by estimating from age, then try small doses upward until a seizure occurs. But treatment is not just about reaching the threshold—the effective dose is usually 2.5 to 5 times the threshold. For bilateral, 2.5 times is enough, while right unilateral requires 5 times, because unilateral stimulation is harder to achieve the same effect. This dose varies from person to person and must be adjusted by trial and error. If a patient has a treatment where the seizure does not occur or does not last long enough (less than 25 seconds), the doctor may increase the dose and try again. Treatments are typically three times a week, with a full course of 6 to 18 sessions, or even longer.

points.h: We still don't know exactly how ECT works
points.body: Why does shocking the brain treat depression and catatonia? Frankly: we still don't fully understand. There are several main hypotheses. One is neurotransmitter changes: after ECT, serotonin, dopamine, and GABA (an inhibitory transmitter) all change significantly. The rise in GABA is itself anticonvulsant, which could explain why the seizure threshold rises and seizures get shorter with consecutive treatments. Second, large fluctuations in hormones such as ACTH, prolactin, and TSH are seen in the hypothalamus and pituitary. Third, ECT promotes neurogenesis, with the key molecule being BDNF (brain-derived neurotrophic factor). But how these changes directly relieve symptoms still lacks a one-to-one mechanism. The mechanisms may also differ for different conditions (depression, schizophrenia, catatonia), and for now we can only continue researching.

points.h: Depression data: far better than first-line antidepressants
points.body: For treating severe depression, the key data for ECT are quite strong: most studies report remission rates (complete disappearance of symptoms) of 50%-60%, and response rates (marked improvement) of 60%-90%. In comparison, the maximum remission rate for SSRI antidepressants is only about 40%. ECT also has a rare benefit—it can halve the 30-day readmission rate. This is not to say it should be first-line, nor that it has no risks (relapse or symptom rebound within 6-12 months is still not uncommon); but in patients with treatment-resistant depression and severe suicide risk, these efficacy advantages are hard to ignore.

points.h: Memory problems are the most concerning side effect
points.body: The most troublesome side effects of ECT center on cognition and memory. Immediately after the procedure there is brief confusion lasting from a few dozen seconds to half an hour, and for weeks there may be decreased attention and executive function. Interestingly, most cognitive functions actually improve in the long term—possibly due to improvement in depression. The real trouble is memory. Anterograde amnesia (difficulty forming new memories) usually recovers within a few weeks after the course ends, so many people are restricted from driving or making major decisions during treatment. Retrograde amnesia (loss of past memories) is what worries patients more: it typically affects recall of the most recent months or even years before treatment, and in most cases recovers, but in some it is permanent. Bilateral treatment is more likely to cause this problem than right unilateral.

points.h: Catatonia: a frequently misidentified fatal syndrome
points.body: Catatonia is often simply classified as a subtype of schizophrenia, but it is actually a psychomotor syndrome that can be triggered by any psychiatric or neurological illness. Patients appear awake, with eyes open, yet are almost completely immobile and mute, and may show posturing, waxy flexibility (an arm placed in a position stays there). Because they cannot eat or drink and are immobile for long periods, they are prone to malnutrition, pressure sores, muscle contractures, and even death. Untreated catatonia can have a mortality rate as high as 20%! The most common treatment is benzodiazepines, but ECT is extremely effective in catatonia from various causes. The girl with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis (the 'Brain on Fire' case) mentioned earlier developed catatonia, and both immunotherapy and lorazepam failed; she ultimately recovered with ECT.

points.h: The biggest bottleneck is not efficacy but access
points.body: Dr. Lopez believes the biggest obstacle ECT currently faces is finding a treatment site. His hospital performs over 6,000 treatments per year across two campuses, averaging about 10-12 treatments per patient. But it is not widely available across the US, and many adult and pediatric patients travel across states to seek care, especially in cases of infants, children, and adolescents with catatonia due to autoimmune encephalitis, where finding an experienced treatment team is extremely difficult. Therefore, improving access is his greatest hope. At the same time, doctors in other internal medicine, pediatric, and critical care teams often do not recognize catatonia and do not dare or think to consult ECT; so 'preaching' to non-psychiatric colleagues is also part of his daily work.

terms.def: A syndrome characterized by marked abnormalities in motor behavior and speech, which can be triggered by various psychiatric or neurological illnesses and can be life-threatening in severe cases.
An autoimmune encephalitis often presenting with seizures, psychiatric symptoms, and catatonia, requiring immunotherapy.
A muscle relaxant used in ECT that blocks neuromuscular transmission to prevent strong generalized convulsions during the electrical stimulus.
Loss of previously formed memories, often for events months to years before ECT.
Uses magnetic pulses to induce weaker currents in the brain without causing seizures; side effects are minor but efficacy is usually weaker than ECT.

When we compare this to SSRIs, which we talked about in a prior episode, they have a remission rate at best of around 40 percent.
The most common indication is for treatment-resistant depression, patients who have depression and have received medication for depression therapy and have not responded and remain ill.
We use it in catatonia, which is a neuropsychiatric condition characterized by changes in speech and motor behavior that sort of spans a number of diagnoses.

The more that we're able to show our colleagues in other fields the value of this treatment, the more they support it. I think that's been a big reason why we have tried at my hospital to sort of be very forward-facing with other departments.
I think the biggest limitation is access to treatment without question.
